name: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah
bio: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah, whose name shows him to have been a Christian, belonged to the Shaiban branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il, in Mesopotamia. Lyall has no information about his date or history.

poems.title: Ode LXXII: O Ka'b ! would that thou
poems.author: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah
poems.note: Lyall's heading: 'Abd al-Masih son of 'Asalah, a man of Murrah, of Dhuhl son of Shaiban, of Bakr.
poems.text:
O Ka'b ! would that thou wouldst restrain thyself to good wine-fellowship, and cease to give offence to thy company,

And be content to listen to the singing-girl who delights us on a cloudy day, so that we go home to rest [well pleased,] as Persian kings are lulled to sleep !

Then wouldst thou be sober [, not drunken as thou art now]. But the man of Namir thinks her [nothing short of] the uncle of Spica Virginis, or the aunt of the Pleiades.

Hold back Ka'b, now that she has given him a buffet on the forehead with a plump wrist !

On his brow are streaks of blood, caked and dry, as the fingers of him that gathers grapes are dyed purple. -

Nay, the wine is not thy brother : sometimes it betrays him that trusts too much to his self-command,

And tempts him with foolish counsel, what time the gust of its intoxication rises to the brain.

I am a man of the house of Murrah : if I wound you [with my satire], ye will not be able to stanch the wound.

poems.title: Ode LXXIII: Often into a far distant meadow
poems.author: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah
poems.text:
Often into a far distant meadow, where the many-coloured bloom tops the quick-growing greenery, and in its glistening dewy brightness the boot profits not the [wearer, who is as good as] bare-footed,

Have I plunged at early dawn with a comrade like a wolf, who rears him-self on high, whose breast [from the pollen of the flowers] is like a perfume-pounder of mother-of-pearl.

So early did I visit it that its sparrows had not yet begun to twitter — my companion striving to conceal himself : but others may be hidden — not he !

But it helps not the wildings that they have warning of his coming : he is as it were suspended over them with a grapnel [to clutch them].

When I endeavour to restrain him, he pushes on, making for them, like the pushing-on of a torrent over the papyrus-stems standing in the way of the flood.

poems.title: Ode LXXXIII: Mayst thou be safe from the
poems.author: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah
poems.text:
Mayst thou be safe from the changes of Time, O Fatimah : and if thou askest me of them, thou askest in me one who knows them well !

We went forth in the morning to meet our foes, and the swords were our staves in our right hands, wherewith we test and try the skulls [of our enemies].

By my life ! we fed full the hyaenas of 'Unaizah for a year with them, and the old and feeble vultures.

[The hyaenas] suck out the marrow from the ends of the long bones in the early morning ; and we print [with our swords] an abiding mark on the noses [of our foes] ;

[And many the man despoiled of his mail-coat and his weapons have we left with the wolf standing over him, tearing his flesh.]

But as for the brother of Qurt, — I am not jesting — say to him : ' Be thou safe, so long as Murrah is safe ! '
